units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Number patterns and flow diagrams
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Mathematics, Term 1: Numeric patterns, including flow diagrams (Patterns, Functions and Algebra)
units.intention: Today I am practising finding the rule in a number pattern.
units.prompt: What stays the same each time?

lesson.say: A number pattern follows a rule. In 4, 8, 12, 16 the rule is add 4 each time.
lesson.html:
A number pattern follows a rule. Look at this pattern:

4→8→12→16

Each number is 4 more than the one before. The rule is add 4. The amount we add each time is called the constant difference.

lesson.say: Some patterns grow by multiplying. In 3, 6, 12, 24 the rule is multiply by 2.
lesson.html:
Some patterns grow faster because they multiply:

3→6→12→24

Each number is double the one before. The rule is multiply by 2. Patterns can also get smaller, by subtracting or dividing.

lesson.say: A flow diagram has an input, a rule and an output. If the rule is times 5, an input of 3 gives an output of 15.
lesson.html:
A flow diagram shows an input, a rule and an output.

3→× 5→15

To find the input when you know the output, work backwards with the opposite operation: 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

steps: Find the difference between the numbers: 14 − 7 = 7, and 21 − 14 = 7.
The difference stays the same, so the rule is add 7.
28 + 7 = 35, and 35 + 7 = 42. The next two numbers are 35 and 42.

questions.q: What is the next number? 5, 10, 15, 20, …
hints: Look at how much the numbers grow each time.
The pattern adds 5 each time. What is 20 + 5?
questions.explain: The rule is add 5, so 20 + 5 = 25.

questions.q: What is the rule? 100, 90, 80, 70
hints: Are the numbers getting bigger or smaller?
The numbers get 10 smaller each time.
questions.explain: Each number is 10 less than the one before, so the rule is subtract 10.

questions.q: The rule is × 4. The input is 6. What is the output?
questions.html: 6→× 4→?

questions.q: The rule is + 25. The output is 75. What was the input?
questions.html: ?→+ 25→75
hints: The opposite of adding is subtracting.
questions.explain: Working backwards, 75 − 25 = 50. Check: 50 + 25 = 75.

questions.q: What number is missing? 3, 6, 12, __, 48
hints: The numbers grow faster each time. Is the pattern adding or multiplying?
questions.explain: The rule is multiply by 2: 12 × 2 = 24, and 24 × 2 = 48.

questions.q: Thandi saves R15 every week. She starts with nothing. How much has she saved after 6 weeks?
hints: The savings make a pattern: R15, R30, R45, …
Keep adding R15 until you have 6 numbers.

reflect.q: What helped you find the rule?

units.parent: Your child practised finding rules in number patterns and flow diagrams, which builds early algebra.
units.teacher: Shows whether the learner finds a constant difference, recognises multiplication patterns and can reverse a flow diagram.
units.done: Number patterns are everywhere: in times tables, calendars and savings.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Folktale: Why Hare Has Long Ears
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 English Home Language, Term 1: Folklore (reading and viewing); language structures: common and proper nouns, adjectives
units.intention: Today I am practising understanding a story and the words that build it.
units.prompt: What caught your attention in the story?
units.passage:
Why Hare Has Long Ears (a 2to.iQ folktale)

Long ago, Hare had short, round ears, just like Mouse. Hare was quick, but he never listened.

One afternoon, Grandmother Tortoise called all the animals together. "Tonight the rain will be heavy," she said slowly. "The river will flood. Move your homes to the high rocks."

All the animals listened, except Hare. He was busy racing his own shadow across the veld.

That night, the water rose higher and higher. Hare woke up wet and cold, and he had to swim all the way to the high rocks.

In the morning, Hare sat shivering beside Tortoise. "I was foolish," he said. "I wish I could hear better."

Tortoise smiled. "Then stretch your ears towards wise words," she said.

So every day, Hare stretched his ears to listen to the wind, the birds and his friends. His ears grew longer and longer. And that is why, to this day, Hare has long ears and hears danger before anyone else.

lesson.say: A folktale is an old story that people told aloud. Folktales often explain why something is the way it is, and they teach a lesson.
lesson.html:
A folktale is an old story that people passed on by telling it aloud. Folktales often:

  • explain why something is the way it is
  • have animals that talk
  • teach a lesson

lesson.say: Read the story. You can press Read aloud to listen to it.
lesson.html:
Why Hare Has Long Ears (a 2to.iQ folktale)

Long ago, Hare had short, round ears, just like Mouse. Hare was quick, but he never listened.

One afternoon, Grandmother Tortoise called all the animals together. "Tonight the rain will be heavy," she said slowly. "The river will flood. Move your homes to the high rocks."

All the animals listened, except Hare. He was busy racing his own shadow across the veld.

That night, the water rose higher and higher. Hare woke up wet and cold, and he had to swim all the way to the high rocks.

In the morning, Hare sat shivering beside Tortoise. "I was foolish," he said. "I wish I could hear better."

Tortoise smiled. "Then stretch your ears towards wise words," she said.

So every day, Hare stretched his ears to listen to the wind, the birds and his friends. His ears grew longer and longer. And that is why, to this day, Hare has long ears and hears danger before anyone else.

lesson.say: A noun names a person, animal, place or thing. A proper noun names a particular one and starts with a capital letter. An adjective describes a noun.
lesson.html:
A noun names a person, animal, place or thing: river, ears, rocks.

A proper noun names a particular person, place or character and starts with a capital letter: Hare, Tortoise, Cape Town.

An adjective describes a noun: short ears, high rocks, wise words.

example.q: Find the adjectives: "Hare woke up wet and cold."
steps: An adjective describes a noun.
Which words tell us what Hare was like?
"Wet" and "cold" describe Hare, so they are adjectives.

questions.q: Who warned the animals about the flood?
hints: Look near the start of the story.
Find who "called all the animals together".
It was the oldest, slowest animal.
questions.explain: Grandmother Tortoise warned them that the river would flood.

questions.q: What was Hare doing while the others listened?
hints: Find the sentence that starts "All the animals listened, except Hare."
He was busy with a game on the veld.
questions.explain: Hare was racing his own shadow across the veld.

questions.q: Put the events in the order they happened.
items: Hare stretches his ears every day
hints: What happens at the very beginning?
The ending explains why Hare's ears are long.
questions.explain: Warning, not listening, the flood, then Hare's ears grow long.

questions.q: Why did Hare say, "I was foolish"?
options: He had not listened to the warning
hints: What happened to Hare that night?
Why did he get wet when the others did not?
He did not move his home because he did not listen.
questions.explain: Hare got wet and cold because he did not listen to Tortoise's warning.

questions.q: What lesson does this folktale teach?
options: Running fast is the most important thing
hints: What did Tortoise tell Hare to do?
questions.explain: The story teaches that it is wise to listen, especially to good advice.

questions.q: Sort the words into nouns and adjectives.
hints: A noun is a thing. An adjective describes a thing.
Can you put "the" in front of it? Then it is probably a noun.
short, cold and wise describe things.
questions.explain: river, ears and rocks are nouns. short, cold and wise are adjectives.

questions.q: Which word is a proper noun in this story?
hints: A proper noun names a particular character.
It starts with a capital letter in the story.
questions.explain: "Tortoise" is used as a character's name, so it is a proper noun with a capital letter.

reflect.q: How did you understand the story best?

units.parent: Your child read a folktale, answered questions about it, and practised nouns and adjectives.
units.teacher: Shows literal recall, sequencing, inference (why Hare felt foolish) and identification of nouns and adjectives. Note whether the learner used the text or read-aloud.
units.done: Folktales carry wisdom from one generation to the next.

units.subject: Natural Sciences and Technology
units.title: Living and non-living things
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Natural Sciences and Technology, Term 1, Life and Living: Living and non-living things; what plants need to grow
units.intention: Today I am practising using evidence to decide if something is living.

lesson.say: All living things carry out seven life processes: they move, breathe, feed, grow, reproduce, excrete waste, and sense and respond.
lesson.html:
All living things carry out seven life processes:

  • Move: even plants move slowly, turning towards light
  • Breathe: take in and give out gases
  • Feed: need food for energy
  • Grow: get bigger and change
  • Reproduce: make young ones or seeds
  • Excrete: get rid of waste
  • Sense and respond: notice and react to their surroundings

lesson.say: Non-living things do not carry out all seven life processes. A car moves and uses fuel, but it cannot grow or reproduce, so it is not living.
lesson.html:
Non-living things do not carry out all seven life processes.

A car moves and uses fuel, but it cannot grow or reproduce, so it is not living. A seed looks still, but it is living: when it gets water and warmth, it grows.

lesson.say: Plants need water, light and air to grow well. Most also need soil for nutrients and to hold their roots.
lesson.html: Plants need water, light and air to grow well. Most plants also grow in soil, which gives them nutrients and holds their roots.

example.q: Is a candle flame living or non-living?
steps: Check the life processes. A flame seems to move and grow, and it needs air.
But it cannot reproduce by itself, and it does not sense and respond like a living thing.
So a candle flame is non-living, even though it shares some features with living things.

questions.q: Sort these into living and non-living.
hints: Ask: does it grow and reproduce?
A mushroom is a fungus. It grows and makes spores.
A cloud moves and changes, but it does not feed or reproduce.
questions.explain: Dogs, trees and mushrooms are living. Rocks, clouds and bicycles are non-living.

questions.q: A plant on a windowsill bends towards the light. Which life process is this?
hints: The plant notices something around it.
questions.explain: The plant senses the light and responds by bending towards it.

questions.q: Why is a car NOT a living thing, even though it moves?
hints: Living things carry out all seven life processes.
Can a car make baby cars?
Can a car get bigger by itself?
questions.explain: A car moves and uses fuel, but it cannot grow or reproduce.

questions.q: A bean seed is kept in a dry box. Is it living?
options: Yes, it can grow when it gets water
hints: Think about what happens when you plant a seed and water it.
A seed is waiting for the right conditions.
It can grow and make a new plant.
questions.explain: A seed is living. It is resting until it gets water and warmth, then it grows.

questions.q: Musa puts one plant in a dark cupboard and one in the sun. Both get the same water. What do you predict?
options: The plant in the sun grows better
The plant in the cupboard grows better
hints: What do plants need to grow?
Which plant has everything it needs?
questions.explain: Plants need light to grow well, so the plant in the sun will grow better. The plant in the dark will turn pale and weak.

questions.q: In Musa's test, why do both plants get the same amount of water?
options: So that light is the only thing that is different
hints: A fair test changes only one thing.
What is Musa trying to find out about?
If water were different too, could we tell what made the difference?
questions.explain: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it is light, so we know light caused any difference.

reflect.q: How did you decide if something was living?
options: Imagined what it does over time

units.parent: Your child used the seven life processes to decide what is living, and thought about a fair test with plants.
units.teacher: Shows classification using criteria, handling of tricky cases (seed, flame, cloud), prediction and an early understanding of fair testing.
units.done: Scientists use evidence, not just how things look, to decide.

units.subject: Life Skills
units.title: My strengths
units.topic: Personal and Social Well-being: personal strengths
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Life Skills, Term 1, Personal and Social Well-being: Personal strengths (own strengths and those of others; using strengths to improve)
units.intention: Today I am practising noticing strengths in myself and in others.
units.prompt: How could a strength help with something hard?

lesson.say: A strength is something you do well, or a good quality you have. Everyone has different strengths.
lesson.html:
A strength is something you do well, or a good quality you have.

  • Things you do well: drawing, building, remembering facts, running, singing
  • Good qualities: being kind, patient, honest, a good listener, a helper

Everyone has strengths, and they are different for each person.

lesson.say: You can use a strength to help with something you find hard. Zizi finds spelling hard, but she is good at drawing. She draws a picture for each spelling word.
lesson.html:
Meet Zizi. She finds spelling hard, but she is very good at drawing. She draws a small picture next to each spelling word, and the pictures help her remember.

When something goes badly, we can learn from it and try a new way.

lesson.say: When we notice and appreciate other people's strengths, we can work well together.
lesson.html: When we notice other people's strengths and tell them, everyone feels respected. A team works best when people use their different strengths.

example.q: Ayanda is very patient. How could this help him in a group project?
steps: Being patient means staying calm and waiting without getting upset.
In a group, people work at different speeds.
Ayanda could help a group member who is slower, calmly and without rushing them.

questions.q: Sort these into things people do well and good qualities.
hints: A quality describes what a person is like.
Things people do well are activities.
Kind, honest and patient describe a person.
questions.explain: Drawing, building and singing are things people do well. Kind, honest and patient are good qualities.

questions.q: Zizi is good at drawing but finds spelling hard. What is a good way for her to use her strength?
options: Draw pictures to help her remember words
hints: Her strength can help with the hard thing.
Which answer uses drawing to help with spelling?
questions.explain: Zizi uses her drawing to help her remember spelling words.

questions.q: Thabo's team lost a soccer match. What could help him learn from it?
options: Think about what to practise next time
hints: A less successful experience can still teach us something.
What can Thabo do to improve?
Which answer looks forward to next time?
questions.explain: Thinking about what to practise turns a loss into learning.

questions.q: Your classmate builds an amazing model. What is a respectful thing to say?
options: "You're really good at building. How did you do it?"
hints: Respect means noticing and valuing someone.
A question shows you are interested.
questions.explain: Naming someone's strength and showing interest is respectful and kind.

questions.q: Which sentence is TRUE?
options: Everyone has strengths, and they can be different
hints: Think about your family and friends.
Do they all do the same things well?
Strengths can be skills or good qualities, and they grow with practice.
questions.explain: Everyone has strengths. They are different for each person and can grow with practice.

questions.q: Choose one strength you have. There is no wrong answer.
options: I am good at making things
hints: What do other people say you do well?
questions.explain: That is a real strength. You can use it to help with things that feel hard.

reflect.q: How did it feel to think about strengths?

units.parent: Your child thought about strengths in themselves and others, and how strengths can help with things that feel hard.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of skills versus qualities, using strengths to improve, and respectful responses. The final choice is the learner's own and is not marked.
units.done: Knowing your strengths helps you learn in your own way.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Place value and rounding
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Mathematics, Term 1: Whole numbers (place value to 4 digits; rounding to the nearest 10, 100 and 1 000; ordering and comparing)
units.intention: Today I am practising what each digit is worth, and rounding numbers.

lesson.say: In 4 735 the 4 is worth 4 thousand, the 7 is worth 7 hundred, the 3 is worth 3 tens, and the 5 is worth 5 units.
lesson.html:
In 4 735, each digit has a place value:

ThousandsHundredsTensUnits
4735

So 4 735 = 4 000 + 700 + 30 + 5. This is called expanded notation. In South Africa we leave a space between the thousands and the hundreds.

lesson.say: To round, look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up. If it is less than 5, round down.
lesson.html:
To round, look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to.

  • 5 or more: round up
  • less than 5: round down

4 735 to the nearest 10 is 4 740. To the nearest 100 it is 4 700. To the nearest 1 000 it is 5 000.

steps: The hundreds digit is 3, so the answer is either 2 300 or 2 400.
Look at the digit to the right: the tens digit is 6.
6 is 5 or more, so round up: 2 368 is 2 400 to the nearest 100.

questions.q: What is the value of the 7 in 4 735?
hints: Find the place the 7 is in.
Count from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands.
The 7 is in the hundreds place.
questions.explain: The 7 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 700.

questions.q: Which shows 6 052 in expanded notation?
hints: Break the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and units.
questions.explain: 6 052 = 6 000 + 50 + 2. There are no hundreds.

questions.q: Round 3 486 to the nearest 10.
hints: The units digit is 6, which is 5 or more.
questions.explain: The units digit is 6, so we round up: 3 490.

questions.q: Round 7 251 to the nearest 1 000.
hints: The hundreds digit is 2, which is less than 5.
questions.explain: The hundreds digit is 2, so we round down to 7 000.

questions.q: Put these numbers in order from smallest to biggest.
questions.explain: 5 093 is less than 5 309, which is less than 5 930.

questions.q: A school has 1 476 learners. To the nearest 100, about how many is that?
hints: The tens digit is 7, so round up.
questions.explain: The tens digit is 7, so 1 476 rounds up to 1 500.

units.parent: Your child worked out what each digit is worth, and rounded numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1 000.
units.teacher: Shows place value understanding to 4 digits, expanded notation, the rounding rule and comparing numbers.
units.done: Rounding helps us estimate quickly, like checking a shop bill.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Halves, quarters and eighths
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Mathematics, Term 2: Common fractions (halves to eighths; comparing and ordering; equivalent fractions; adding with the same denominator)
units.intention: Today I am practising naming, comparing and finding equal fractions.
units.prompt: How did the picture help you?

lesson.say: A fraction is part of a whole that has been cut into equal parts. Three quarters means 3 out of 4 equal parts.
lesson.html:
A fraction is part of a whole cut into equal parts.

This shows 3/4: 3 out of 4 equal parts.

lesson.say: One half, two quarters and four eighths are equal. They cover the same amount.
lesson.html: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. These are equivalent fractions: they cover the same amount.

steps: Both fractions have 2 parts.
Thirds are bigger than fifths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts.
So 2/3 is bigger than 2/5.

questions.q: What fraction is shaded?
questions.html: <svg width="100%" style="max-width:300px" viewBox="0 0 300 44" role="img" aria-label="3 out of 8 parts shaded"><rect x="1" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--shape-a)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="38.5" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--shape-a)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="76" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--shape-a)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="113.5" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--surface)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="151" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--surface)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="188.5" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--surface)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="226" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--surface)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/><rect x="263.5" y="2" width="35.5" height="40" rx="4" fill="var(--surface)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-opacity="0.5"/></svg>
questions.explain: 3 out of 8 equal parts are shaded: 3/8.

questions.q: Which is bigger: 1/3 or 1/7?
hints: Which whole is cut into fewer pieces?
questions.explain: A third is bigger than a seventh.

questions.q: Which fraction is equal to 1/2?
hints: Look at the fraction bars on the lesson page.
2 out of 4 is the same as half.
questions.explain: 2/4 covers the same amount as 1/2.

questions.q: Put these in order from smallest to biggest.
hints: The bigger the denominator, the smaller the part.
questions.explain: 1/8 is smaller than 1/4, which is smaller than 1/2.

questions.q: Mama cuts a loaf into 8 equal slices. The family eats 5 slices. What fraction of the loaf is left?
hints: How many slices were there altogether?
questions.explain: 8 − 5 = 3 slices are left: 3/8 of the loaf.

reflect.q: How did you work out the fractions?

units.parent: Your child named fractions, compared them and found fractions that are equal.
units.teacher: Shows part-whole understanding, comparison of unit fractions, early equivalence and adding like fractions.
units.done: Fractions are all around us: in food, time and money.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Poetry: Rain on the Roof
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 English Home Language, Term 1: Poetry (reading and viewing); rhyme, rhythm, repetition and sound words
units.intention: Today I am practising enjoying a poem and noticing how it uses sounds.
units.prompt: Which line could you hear in your head?
units.passage:
Rain on the Roof (a 2to.iQ poem)

Tap-tap, tip-tap, the rain begins to fall,
It drums upon the tin roof and patters down the wall.
The thirsty garden opens up, the dusty road turns brown,
And all the little puddles shine like silver in the town.

Tap-tap, tip-tap, the clouds roll slowly by,
And then the sun peeps out again to dry the morning sky.

lesson.say: Read the poem, or press Read aloud to listen.
lesson.html:
Rain on the Roof (a 2to.iQ poem)

Tap-tap, tip-tap, the rain begins to fall,
It drums upon the tin roof and patters down the wall.
The thirsty garden opens up, the dusty road turns brown,
And all the little puddles shine like silver in the town.

Tap-tap, tip-tap, the clouds roll slowly by,
And then the sun peeps out again to dry the morning sky.

lesson.say: Poems often rhyme. They have a beat called rhythm. They repeat words. And they use sound words like tap and drum.
lesson.html:
• Rhyme: words that end with the same sound, like fall and wall
  • Rhythm: the beat you hear when you read it aloud
  • Repetition: words used again, like tap-tap, tip-tap
  • Sound words: words that sound like the noise they describe, like tap, drum and patter

example.q: Find a word that rhymes with "brown".
steps: Find "brown" at the end of line 3.
Look at the end of the next line.
"Town" ends with the same sound, so "brown" and "town" rhyme.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with "fall"?
hints: Look at the end of line 2.
Rhyming words end with the same sound.
questions.explain: "Fall" and "wall" rhyme.

questions.q: Which of these is a sound word?
hints: A sound word sounds like the noise it describes.
Which word sounds like rain hitting something?
questions.explain: "Patters" sounds like light rain landing.

questions.q: What does "the thirsty garden" mean?
hints: Can a garden really be thirsty?
What happens to a garden when there is no rain?
The rain gives the garden what it needs.
questions.explain: The poet means the dry garden needed water.

questions.q: Why does the poet repeat "Tap-tap, tip-tap"?
questions.explain: The repeated words sound like raindrops falling.

questions.q: Put these in the order they happen in the poem.
hints: The sun appears at the end.
questions.explain: Rain, puddles, clouds moving away, then the sun.

reflect.q: How did you enjoy the poem most?

units.parent: Your child read a poem about rain and noticed rhyme, repetition and sound words.
units.teacher: Shows identification of rhyme and onomatopoeia, interpretation of figurative language, and sequencing within a poem.
units.done: Poems let us hear and picture the world in new ways.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Instructions: Grow a bean in a jar
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 English Home Language, Term 1: Instructional text (reading and viewing); command verbs and sequence words
units.intention: Today I am practising following and understanding instructions.
units.prompt: What would happen if you skipped a step?
units.passage:
How to Grow a Bean in a Jar

You will need: a clean glass jar, two paper towels, water and two bean seeds.

  1. First, fold the paper towels and press them around the inside of the jar.
  2. Next, push the bean seeds between the glass and the paper, so that you can see them.
  3. Then pour a little water into the jar to make the paper damp, but not soaking.
  4. Put the jar in a warm place that gets some light.
  5. Finally, check your beans every day. Add a little water if the paper feels dry.

After a few days, you should see roots growing from the beans.

lesson.say: Instructions tell you how to do something. They have a title, a list of what you need, and numbered steps.
lesson.html:
Instructions tell you how to do something. They usually have:

  • a title that says what you will make or do
  • a "You will need" list
  • numbered steps in order
  • sequence words: first, next, then, finally
  • command verbs at the start: fold, push, pour

lesson.say: Read the instructions for growing a bean in a jar.
lesson.html:
How to Grow a Bean in a Jar

You will need: a clean glass jar, two paper towels, water and two bean seeds.

  1. First, fold the paper towels and press them around the inside of the jar.
  2. Next, push the bean seeds between the glass and the paper, so that you can see them.
  3. Then pour a little water into the jar to make the paper damp, but not soaking.
  4. Put the jar in a warm place that gets some light.
  5. Finally, check your beans every day. Add a little water if the paper feels dry.

After a few days, you should see roots growing from the beans.

example.q: Find the command verb in: "Pour a little water into the jar."
steps: A command verb tells you what to do.
It is usually the first word of the step.
"Pour" is the command verb.

questions.q: What is the purpose of this text?
options: To tell you how to grow a bean
To tell a story about a bean
hints: Does it tell a story, or tell you what to do?
questions.explain: It tells you how to grow a bean in a jar.

questions.q: Put the steps in the right order.
items: Fold the paper towels into the jar
Put the jar in a warm place
hints: The jar needs paper before the beans go in.
questions.explain: Paper, beans, water, then a warm place.

questions.q: Sort these words: command verbs or sequence words.
hints: A command verb tells you to do something.
first, next and finally show order.
questions.explain: fold, pour and check are command verbs. first, next and finally are sequence words.

questions.q: Why are the steps numbered?
options: So you do them in the right order
hints: Could you water the beans before putting them in?
questions.explain: The numbers help you do the steps in the right order.

questions.q: The paper towel feels dry. What should you do?
options: Put the jar in the fridge
hints: What does it say to do when the paper is dry?
questions.explain: Step 5 says to add a little water if the paper feels dry.

reflect.q: What helped you follow the instructions?

units.parent: Your child read instructions, put steps in order and found command verbs and sequence words.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of the structure and purpose of procedural text, sequencing, and grammatical features (imperatives, connectives).
units.done: Good instructions are clear, short and in the right order.

units.subject: Natural Sciences and Technology
units.title: Habitats of animals
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Natural Sciences and Technology, Term 1, Life and Living: Habitats of animals (different habitats; the need for a habitat)
units.intention: Today I am practising explaining why animals live where they do.
units.prompt: What does the animal need from its home?

lesson.say: A habitat is the place where an animal lives. It gives the animal food, water, shelter and space to raise its young.
lesson.html:
A habitat is the place where an animal lives. A good habitat gives an animal:

  • food and water
  • shelter from weather and danger
  • space to move and to raise its young

lesson.say: South Africa has many habitats, such as grasslands, forests, deserts, wetlands and the ocean.
lesson.html:
• Grassland: zebra, springbok
  • Forest: monkeys, many birds
  • Desert, like the Kalahari: gemsbok, meerkats
  • Wetland or pond: frogs, ducks
  • Ocean: dolphins, fish, penguins on the shore

Animals have body parts and habits that suit their habitat. A frog needs water to lay its eggs.

example.q: Why do frogs live near ponds?
steps: Think about what a frog needs.
Frogs lay their eggs in water, and tadpoles live in water.
Frogs also catch insects that live near water. So a pond gives them water, food and a place to breed.

questions.q: Sort the animals into their main habitat.
hints: Which animals need to live in water all the time?
Frogs and ducks live in or near ponds.
questions.explain: Dolphins and fish live in the ocean, gemsbok and meerkats in the desert, frogs and ducks in wetlands.

questions.q: Which of these does a habitat NOT need to give an animal?
hints: Think about what animals need to survive.
Which one is a human object?
questions.explain: Animals need food, water, shelter and space. They do not need a television.

questions.q: A wetland is drained to build houses. What will happen to the frogs?
options: They lose their habitat and may die or move
They will live in the houses
They will learn to swim in the sea
hints: What do frogs need water for?
Where will they lay their eggs?
Without water, the habitat is gone.
questions.explain: The frogs lose the water they need, so they must move or they may die.

questions.q: Why can a gemsbok survive in the Kalahari?
options: It can go a long time without drinking water
It needs to swim every day
hints: What is scarce in a desert?
Desert animals are suited to dry places.
Gemsbok get much of their water from the plants they eat.
questions.explain: Gemsbok can survive a long time without drinking, which suits the dry Kalahari.

questions.q: Why do different animals live in different habitats?
options: Each animal is suited to the place that meets its needs
hints: Think about the frog and the gemsbok.
A habitat must give an animal what it needs.
questions.explain: Each animal's body and habits suit the habitat that gives it food, water and shelter.

units.parent: Your child learnt what a habitat is and why animals live where they do.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of animal needs, classification by habitat, and reasoning about the effects of habitat loss.
units.done: Protecting habitats protects the animals that live in them.

units.subject: Natural Sciences and Technology
units.title: Solids, liquids and gases
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Natural Sciences and Technology, Term 2, Matter and Materials: Materials around us (solids, liquids and gases)
units.intention: Today I am practising sorting materials by how they behave.
units.prompt: What did you notice about its shape?

lesson.say: Materials can be solid, liquid or gas. Solids keep their shape. Liquids flow and take the shape of their container. Gases spread out to fill any space.
lesson.html:
• Solids keep their own shape: a stone, a spoon, ice
  • Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, but keep the same amount: water, milk, cooking oil
  • Gases spread out to fill all the space they are in: air, steam

lesson.say: Heating ice makes it melt into water. Heating water makes it boil and become steam. Cooling water makes it freeze.
lesson.html:
ice (solid)→water (liquid)→steam (gas)

Heating melts ice into water and boils water into steam. Cooling turns steam back into water and freezes water into ice.

example.q: Is sand a solid or a liquid? It can be poured.
steps: Look at one grain of sand.
Each grain keeps its own shape, so each grain is a solid.
Sand pours because it is made of many tiny solid pieces. So sand is a solid.

questions.q: Sort these into solids, liquids and gases.
hints: Does it keep its own shape?
Does it flow and take the shape of a cup?
Does it spread out and fill a space?
questions.explain: Stone and ice are solids, milk and oil are liquids, air and steam are gases.

questions.q: You pour juice from a bottle into a glass. What happens to its shape?
options: It takes the shape of the glass
hints: Liquids take the shape of their container.
questions.explain: Liquids take the shape of their container, so the juice takes the shape of the glass.

questions.q: What fills a balloon when you blow it up?
hints: What comes out of your mouth when you blow?
It spreads out to fill the balloon.
questions.explain: Air is a gas. It spreads out to fill the balloon.

questions.q: An ice block is left in the sun. What happens?
hints: Heating a solid can change its state.
questions.explain: Heat from the sun melts the solid ice into liquid water.

questions.q: Put these in order as water is heated.
questions.explain: Ice melts into water, and water boils into steam.

reflect.q: How did you decide the state?
options: Things I have seen at home

units.parent: Your child sorted materials into solids, liquids and gases and thought about how heating changes them.
units.teacher: Shows classification by observable properties, handling of a tricky case (sand), and understanding of changes of state.
units.done: Everything around us is a solid, a liquid or a gas.

units.subject: Life Skills
units.title: Respecting my body and others' bodies
units.topic: Personal and Social Well-being: respect for own and others' bodies
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Life Skills, Term 1, Personal and Social Well-being: Respect for own and others' bodies (caring for the body, privacy, avoiding harmful substances)
units.intention: Today I am practising ways to care for my body and respect other people's bodies.
units.prompt: Who could you talk to about that?

lesson.say: We care for our bodies by washing, eating healthy food, sleeping enough and moving every day.
lesson.html:
• Wash your hands and body, and brush your teeth
  • Eat healthy food and drink clean water
  • Sleep enough
  • Move and play every day
  • Only take medicine from a parent, carer or nurse

lesson.say: Your body belongs to you. Private parts are the parts covered by a swimming costume. It is okay to say no. If anything makes you feel unsafe or confused, tell a grown-up you trust.
lesson.html:
Your body belongs to you. The parts covered by a swimming costume are private.

  • It is okay to say no to touch you do not want, even from someone you know
  • There should be no secrets about touching
  • If anything makes you feel unsafe or confused, tell a grown-up you trust, and keep telling until someone helps

Respect other people's bodies too: ask before you hug, and stop when someone says no.

example.q: Someone at the park offers Lindo some pills and says they will make him feel great. What should he do?
steps: Only a parent, carer or nurse should give medicine.
Lindo should say no and walk away.
Then he should tell a trusted grown-up what happened.

questions.q: Sort these: caring for my body, or not caring for my body?
items: Staying up very late every night
hints: Medicine should only come from a trusted adult.
questions.explain: Washing hands and drinking clean water care for the body. Too little sleep and pills from a stranger do not.

questions.q: A friend wants a hug, but Nomsa does not want one today. What is true?
options: It is okay for Nomsa to say no
Nomsa should keep it a secret
hints: Who does Nomsa's body belong to?
She can say no kindly, like "Can we high-five instead?"
questions.explain: Nomsa's body belongs to her, so she can say no. A good friend will respect that.

questions.q: Someone asks a child to keep a secret about touching. What should the child do?
hints: Who can help keep children safe?
A trusted grown-up, like a parent or teacher.
questions.explain: There should be no secrets about touching. The child should tell a trusted grown-up.

questions.q: How can you show respect for someone else's body?
options: Ask before you hug, and stop if they say no
Push them when you are cross
Tease them about how they look
hints: Respect means caring how others feel.
Stopping when someone says no shows respect.
questions.explain: Asking first and stopping when someone says no shows respect.

questions.q: If a trusted grown-up does not listen the first time, what should you do?
hints: Think of other adults you trust.
A teacher, a relative, a nurse.
questions.explain: Keep telling different trusted grown-ups until someone helps.

reflect.q: Who are trusted grown-ups you could talk to?
options: I'd like help to think of one

units.parent: Your child learnt about caring for their body, privacy, saying no and telling a trusted grown-up. Please talk about this together at home.
units.teacher: Protective, scenario-based content. If a learner discloses anything during or after this lesson, follow your school's safeguarding procedure. The final reflection is not marked.
units.done: Your body belongs to you, and there is always someone who can help.

units.subject: Life Skills
units.title: Dealing with conflict
units.topic: Personal and Social Well-being: dealing with conflict
units.caps: CAPS Grade 4 Life Skills, Term 1, Personal and Social Well-being: Dealing with conflict (at home and at school; ways to avoid and respond to conflict)
units.intention: Today I am practising calm ways to sort out disagreements.
units.prompt: How might the other person feel?

lesson.say: Conflict is a disagreement or fight between people. It happens at home and at school. It is normal, but how we deal with it matters.
lesson.html: Conflict is a disagreement between people. It happens at home and at school, for example over toys, turns, or hurtful words. Conflict is normal. What matters is how we deal with it.

lesson.say: Stop and calm down. Say how you feel using I statements. Listen to the other person. Find a solution together. Ask a grown-up for help if you need it.
lesson.html:
1. Stop and calm down
  2. Say how you feel: "I feel upset when…"
  3. Listen to the other person
  4. Find a solution together: take turns, share, or say sorry
  5. Ask a grown-up for help if you need it

example.q: Two friends both want the same swing. What could they do?
steps: Stop and stay calm, without pushing.
Each says what they want: "I really want a turn."
Agree on a solution: take turns, for example counting to 50 each.

questions.q: Which is an "I statement"?
options: "I feel sad when you take my pencil."
hints: An I statement starts with "I feel…".
It talks about your feeling, not blaming.
questions.explain: "I feel sad when…" explains your feeling without blaming.

questions.q: Put the steps for sorting out conflict in order.
hints: You need to be calm before talking.
Then each person speaks and listens.
questions.explain: Calm down, say how you feel, listen, then find a solution together.

questions.q: Sort these responses to conflict.
hints: Helpful responses solve the problem safely.
Does it make things better or worse?
Hitting and name-calling make things worse.
questions.explain: Taking turns, talking and asking for help are helpful. Hitting, name-calling and ignoring for ever are not.

questions.q: Sipho bumps into Ayanda and her tower falls. Sipho didn't mean it. What could Ayanda do?
options: Take a breath and say, "Please be careful. Can you help me rebuild it?"
hints: Which answer is calm and helps solve it?
Asking for help to fix it is a solution.
questions.explain: Calmly explaining and asking for help turns the accident into teamwork.

questions.q: How can you avoid some conflicts before they start?
options: Share, take turns and speak kindly
hints: Many conflicts are about sharing and turns.
questions.explain: Sharing, taking turns and kind words prevent many conflicts.

reflect.q: Which step would help you most?

units.parent: Your child practised calm ways to sort out disagreements, like I statements and taking turns.
units.teacher: Scenario-based. Shows knowledge of conflict-resolution steps, assertive language and the difference between helpful and harmful responses.
units.done: Calm words solve more problems than angry ones.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Multiplication with arrays
units.caps: Cambridge Primary Mathematics (0096), Stage 4: Number (multiplication facts; arrays; commutativity)
units.intention: Today I am using arrays to understand multiplication.
units.prompt: How could you count the eggs in a tray quickly?

lesson.say: An array is objects in rows and columns. 3 rows of 4 is 3 times 4, which is 12.
lesson.html:
🍎🍎🍎🍎
🍎🍎🍎🍎
🍎🍎🍎🍎

3 × 4 = 12

lesson.say: Turn the array on its side: 4 rows of 3. It is still 12. Multiplication works in any order.
If you know 5 times 6 is 30, then 6 times 6 is one more 6: 36.

example.q: An egg tray has 5 rows of 6 eggs. How many eggs?
steps: 5 rows of 6.
30 eggs.

questions.q: 4 rows of 5 chairs. How many chairs?
What is 7 × 3?
Which is the same as 6 × 8?
questions.explain: Multiplication works in any order.

questions.q: You know 10 × 7 = 70. What is 9 × 7?

units.parent: Your child used arrays to multiply and to work out new facts.
units.teacher: Shows representing multiplication as arrays, using commutativity and deriving facts from known facts.
units.done: Rows × columns. Turn it around: same answer.

units.subject: English
units.title: Writing instructions
units.caps: Cambridge Primary English (0058), Stage 4: Writing (instructional texts: imperative verbs, numbered steps and sequencing words)
units.intention: Today I am writing clear instructions.
units.prompt: Could you explain how to make a sandwich?

lesson.say: Instructions have a title, a list of what you need, and numbered steps in order.
lesson.html: Title→You will need→Numbered steps

lesson.say: Each step starts with a command verb, sometimes called a bossy verb: cut, mix, pour, spread.
lesson.html: Spread the butter. Add the cheese.

lesson.say: Order words help the reader follow along: first, next, then, finally.
lesson.html: First→Next→Then→Finally

example.q: Write the first step for making tea.
steps: Think about what happens first.
Start with a command verb.
'1. Boil the water.'

questions.q: Which is a command verb?
hints: It tells you to do something.
questions.explain: 'Mix' tells the reader what to do.

questions.q: Which instruction is clearest?
options: Pour the milk into the glass.
hints: It tells you exactly what to do.
questions.explain: It is a clear command.

questions.q: Put the steps for a sandwich in order.
questions.explain: Bread, butter, filling, close.

questions.q: Why are instruction steps numbered?
options: So the reader follows the right order
questions.explain: Numbers show the order to follow.

units.parent: Your child wrote clear, step-by-step instructions.
units.teacher: Shows structuring instructional texts with imperative verbs, numbered steps and sequencing connectives.
units.done: Title, what you need, then numbered steps starting with command verbs.

units.subject: Science
units.title: Solids, liquids and gases
units.caps: Cambridge Primary Science (0097), Stage 4: Chemistry (solids, liquids and gases; melting and freezing)
units.intention: Today I am sorting things into solids, liquids and gases.
units.prompt: What happens to an ice block on a hot day?

lesson.say: Solids keep their shape. A stone, a book and ice are solids.
lesson.html: 🪨 📕 🧊

lesson.say: Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, like water and juice. Gases spread out to fill any space, like the air in a balloon.
lesson.html: Liquid: flows→Gas: spreads out

lesson.say: Heating can melt a solid into a liquid. Cooling can freeze a liquid into a solid. Ice melts into water; water freezes into ice.
lesson.html: Ice→melts→Water→freezes→Ice

example.q: Is honey a solid, a liquid or a gas?
steps: Honey flows, slowly.
It takes the shape of the jar.
Honey is a liquid.

questions.q: Which is a solid?
questions.explain: A stone keeps its shape.

questions.q: Which is a gas?
questions.explain: Air is a gas.

questions.q: What happens to ice when it is heated?
questions.explain: Heat melts ice into water.

questions.q: Sort them.
hints: Brick and spoon keep their shape.
questions.explain: Milk and juice are liquids; the brick and spoon are solids.

units.parent: Your child sorted materials into solids, liquids and gases.
units.teacher: Shows classifying materials by state and describing melting and freezing.
units.done: Solids keep their shape, liquids flow, gases spread out.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Fractions of a whole
units.caps: IB PYP Mathematics: number (fractions as equal parts of a whole and of a set)
units.intention: Today I am finding fractions of shapes and groups.
units.prompt: How would you share a pizza fairly among four friends?

lesson.say: Central idea: Fractions help us share things fairly. Key concept: Function. Today we are principled.
lesson.html:
Central idea: Fractions help us share things fairly.

Key concept: Function · Learner profile: Principled

lesson.say: A fraction is part of a whole that is split into equal parts. A pizza cut into 4 equal slices: each slice is one quarter.
lesson.html:
🍕

4 equal parts: each is 1/4

lesson.say: To find a fraction of a group, divide by the bottom number. One third of 12 sweets is 12 divided by 3, which is 4.

steps: 2/5 is two of those.

questions.q: A cake is cut into 8 equal pieces. What fraction is one piece?
questions.explain: One of 8 equal parts is 1/8.

questions.q: What is 1/4 of 16?
What is 3/4 of 12?
Why must the parts be equal?
questions.explain: Fractions only work when the parts are equal.

units.parent: Your child found fractions of shapes and groups.
units.teacher: Shows understanding fractions as equal parts and finding unit and non-unit fractions of sets (principled: fair sharing).
units.done: Fractions are equal parts. Divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top.

units.subject: Language
units.title: Persuasive posters
units.caps: IB PYP Language: writing and visual language (persuasive posters: slogans, images and reasons)
units.intention: Today I am designing a poster that persuades.
units.prompt: Which poster has made you want to do something?

lesson.say: Central idea: We can use words and images to persuade others to act. Key concept: Causation. Today we are communicators.
lesson.html:
Central idea: We can use words and images to persuade others to act.

Key concept: Causation · Learner profile: Communicators

lesson.say: A slogan is short and catchy: Turn it off! Save power!
lesson.html: Turn it off! Save power!

lesson.say: A good poster has a clear picture, a reason, and tells people exactly what to do.
lesson.html: Slogan→Picture→Reason→What to do

example.q: Write a slogan for a poster about picking up litter.
steps: Keep it short.
Make it catchy.
'Bin it, don't drop it!'

questions.q: Which is the best slogan?
options: Litter exists in many places around the school grounds.
questions.explain: It is short, catchy and tells people what to do.

questions.q: What should a persuasive poster tell people?
hints: Persuade means get them to act.
questions.explain: It should give a clear action.

questions.q: Why add a picture?
questions.explain: Pictures catch attention fast.

questions.q: Which reason best persuades people to save water?
options: 'Every drop we save helps our town in a drought.'
questions.explain: It gives a real reason that matters.

units.parent: Your child designed a persuasive poster with a slogan, image and reason.
units.teacher: Shows combining slogans, images and reasons to persuade an audience to act (communicator).
units.done: Catchy slogan, clear picture, a reason, and what to do.

units.subject: Science
units.title: Simple machines
units.caps: IB PYP Science, transdisciplinary theme 'How the world works': simple machines (levers, wheels, ramps) make work easier
units.intention: Today I am finding out how simple machines make work easier.
units.prompt: How would you lift something too heavy to carry?

lesson.say: Our theme is How the world works. Central idea: People use simple machines to make work easier. Key concept: Function. Today we are thinkers.
lesson.html:
Central idea: People use simple machines to make work easier.

Key concept: Function · Learner profile: Thinkers

lesson.say: A lever is a bar that turns on a point called a fulcrum. A see-saw and a bottle opener are levers.
lesson.html: See-saw→Bottle opener→Wheelbarrow

lesson.say: A ramp lets you push something up gradually instead of lifting it straight up. Wheels make it easier to move heavy loads.
lesson.html: Ramp: less effort→Wheel: rolls the load

example.q: Why is a wheelbarrow easier than carrying bricks?
steps: The wheel rolls, so you don't drag the load.
The handles act as a lever.
Together they make the load feel lighter to move.

questions.q: Which is a lever?
questions.explain: A see-saw turns on a fulcrum.

questions.q: What is a fulcrum?
options: The point a lever turns on
questions.explain: The fulcrum is the turning point of a lever.

questions.q: Why use a ramp to load a heavy box onto a truck?
options: It takes less effort than lifting straight up
questions.explain: A ramp spreads the effort over a longer distance.

questions.q: What do wheels help with?
questions.explain: Wheels roll, making loads easier to move.

units.parent: Your child explored how levers, ramps and wheels make work easier.
units.teacher: How the world works: shows identifying simple machines and explaining how they reduce effort (thinker).
units.done: Levers, ramps and wheels make work easier.
